title: Penguin bills in Python
text:
Bill measurements are one of the classic ways to tell penguin species apart. Here I check how well bill length and depth separate them, using Python.
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER (CC0 licence). Loaded from the palmerpenguins Python package.

title: Penguin bills in Python
text:
Loading and tidying

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()
bills = penguins.dropna(subset=["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"])

print(len(penguins), "penguins,", len(bills), "with complete bill measurements")

344 penguins, 342 with complete bill measurements

title: Penguin bills in Python
text:
Summary by species

bills.groupby("species")[["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]].mean().round(1)








bill_length_mm
bill_depth_mm


species






Adelie
38.8
18.3


Chinstrap
48.8
18.4


Gentoo
47.5
15.0







Adelie penguins have the shortest bills, Chinstrap the longest, and Gentoo bills are noticeably shallower than the other two.

title: Penguin bills in Python
text:
Bill length versus depth

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for species, group in bills.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(group["bill_length_mm"], group["bill_depth_mm"],
               label=species, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Bill depth (mm)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Bill length versus bill depth, coloured by species.





Figure 1 shows three fairly distinct clusters. Overall the trend between length and depth looks negative, but that is an illusion of pooling: within each species the relationship is positive.

bills.groupby("species").apply(
    lambda g: g["bill_length_mm"].corr(g["bill_depth_mm"]),
    include_groups=False,
).round(2)

species
Adelie       0.39
Chinstrap    0.65
Gentoo       0.64
dtype: float64


This is Simpson’s paradox in a small, friendly form: the pooled correlation and the within-species correlations have opposite signs.

title: R and Python in one post
text:
R and Python are often treated as rivals, but they can share one document. Here I use each for the part it does comfortably: R to load and tidy the Palmer Penguins data, Python (pandas) to summarise it, and R again to plot the result. The reticulate package hands the objects back and forth.
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER (CC0 licence). Loaded from the palmerpenguins R package.

title: R and Python in one post
section: Pointing R at the Python environment
text:
Pointing R at the Python environment
reticulate needs to know which Python to use. I point it at the uv environment in .venv, so the post uses the same packages as the Python post.

library(reticulate)

venv_python <- file.path(Sys.getenv("QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR", "."), ".venv", "bin", "python")
if (file.exists(venv_python)) use_python(venv_python, required = TRUE)

py_config()$version

[1] '3.14'

title: R and Python in one post
text:
R: load and tidy

library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm))

dim(penguins_clean)

[1] 342   8

title: R and Python in one post
text:
Python: summarise
In a Python chunk, the R object is available as r.penguins_clean, and reticulate has already converted it to a pandas DataFrame.

import pandas as pd

df = r.penguins_clean
print(type(df))

<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>

summary = (
    df.groupby("species", observed=True)
    .agg(n=("body_mass_g", "size"),
         mean_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean"),
         mean_flipper_mm=("flipper_length_mm", "mean"))
    .round(1)
    .reset_index()
)
summary

     species    n  mean_mass_g  mean_flipper_mm
0     Adelie  151       3700.7            190.0
1  Chinstrap   68       3733.1            195.8
2     Gentoo  123       5076.0            217.2

title: R and Python in one post
text:
R: plot what Python made
Back in R, the Python object is py$summary, which arrives as an ordinary data frame.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(py$summary, aes(x = species, y = mean_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Mean body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Mean body mass by species, computed in Python and plotted in R.





Figure 1 crosses the language boundary twice: the data went from R to Python, and the summary came back to R for plotting. Gentoo are again the heaviest species by a wide margin.

# A deliberate warning, left visible on purpose: as.integer() on a species name
as.integer(as.character(py$summary$species[1]))

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion


[1] NA


That warning is expected. It is a reminder that values passed between the languages keep their types, so a text column will not quietly become a number.

title: Penguin body mass in R
text:
Which of the three Palmer penguin species is the heaviest, and does body mass track flipper length? I use R to find out.
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER (CC0 licence). Loaded from the palmerpenguins R package.

title: Penguin body mass in R
text:
Loading and tidying

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm))

nrow(penguins)

[1] 344

nrow(penguins_clean)

[1] 342


Removing rows with missing mass or flipper length drops a couple of birds, and leaves the rest of the data intact.

title: Penguin body mass in R
text:
Mass by species

penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_mass_g = round(mean(body_mass_g)),
    sd_mass_g = round(sd(body_mass_g))
  )

# A tibble: 3 x 4
  species       n mean_mass_g sd_mass_g
  <fct>     <int>       <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Adelie      151        3701       459
2 Chinstrap    68        3733       384
3 Gentoo      123        5076       504


Gentoo penguins are clearly the heaviest, about 1.4 kg more than Adelie or Chinstrap on average. Adelie and Chinstrap are close to each other.

ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Body mass of penguins by species.





Figure 1 shows the same story: the Gentoo box sits well above the other two with barely any overlap.

title: Penguin body mass in R
text:
Mass versus flipper length

cor(penguins_clean$body_mass_g, penguins_clean$flipper_length_mm)

[1] 0.8712018


The correlation is strongly positive, so heavier penguins do tend to have longer flippers. This is a quick look and not a model, but it matches what the box plot suggested: much of the difference is between species, and Gentoo is simply a bigger bird.

title: First week of MDS
text:
Exciting, challenging, and overwhelming - sometimes all three before lunch.



Peanut, my dog, who I miss while I get lost on campus.


Figuring out course logistics, labs, exploring the campus and meeting batchmates has been both fun and daunting. There’s a particular kind of low-grade anxiety that comes from suspecting you’ve missed an announcement somewhere.
Campus is still a puzzle. I’ve walked past the same building twice looking for it more than once.
The batchmates have been the best surprise. Everyone arrived from somewhere different - different degrees, different countries, different reasons for being here - and there’s a nice levelling effect in all of us being equally lost in the first week.
Daunting and fun are apparently not opposites. On to week two.
